passage: The shehnai was so loud in the wedding hall that Zubin, fifteen, could hardly hear his great-aunt, but he heard enough. "No God, no prayer, no shame in you," she said, wagging a finger. "Children without belief go astray." A cousin snickered. Zubin's face went hot. The baraat was due in ten minutes and the whole family was rushing. He didn't argue. He lifted a heavy tray of sweets from an old uncle's arms and carried it to the mandap, then fetched water for the musicians. Urmila, his cousin, caught up with him behind a pillar, her bangles clinking. "That wasn't fair. I saw you helping everyone." "I just think it's honest to say I don't know," Zubin said quietly. "You should tell her that yourself, kindly," Urmila said. "I'll sit with you when you do."

qa.q: What did Zubin carry to the mandap?
qa.a: Zubin carried a heavy tray of sweets to the mandap.

qa.q: How does Zubin feel after his great-aunt's remark, and what shows it?
qa.a: Zubin feels ashamed and stung. His face goes hot, and he does not argue, only quietly goes to help.

qa.q: Which choice by Zubin showed that values do not depend on belief?
qa.a: Instead of arguing, Zubin lifted the tray of sweets from the old uncle and fetched water for the musicians, helping people kindly.

qa.q: How does Urmila see what happened?
qa.a: Urmila sees it as unfair. She saw Zubin helping everyone, and she offers to sit with him when he explains himself kindly to his great-aunt.

grounding: A teenager who does not follow any religion is told by a relative that he will go astray, and shows kindness and honesty instead of shame.

passage: At the canteen in their Delhi school, Pranav pointed his samosa at Pankaj. "You don't believe in anything? Then you're lost, yaar. No God means no morals." A few classmates laughed. Pankaj, fifteen, felt heat in his ears. He said, "I'm not lost. I just don't believe in a god. I still think you shouldn't steal or hurt people." Pranav rolled his eyes. That afternoon, when Pranav dropped his wallet in the corridor, Pankaj ran after him to return it and said nothing more about it. At home that night Pankaj told his father, who put down the newspaper. "Honest thinking is nothing to be ashamed of," he said. "And nobody gets to call you a lesser person for it." Pankaj slept better that night.

qa.q: What did Pankaj do when Pranav dropped his wallet?
qa.a: Pankaj ran after Pranav to return the wallet and said nothing more about it.

qa.q: How does Pankaj feel when Pranav calls him lost, and what shows it?
qa.a: Pankaj feels embarrassed and stung. Heat rises in his ears, but he still answers calmly.

qa.q: What turning point helped Pankaj feel better that night?
qa.a: Pankaj told his father, who said that honest thinking is nothing to be ashamed of and that nobody may call him a lesser person for it.

qa.q: How might Pranav have felt when Pankaj returned the wallet?
qa.a: Probably surprised, since the classmate he had mocked had just been kind, which shows conduct can matter more than belief.

grounding: A teenager who does not follow any religion is called lost by a classmate, shows kindness and honesty in conduct, and is supported by a parent.

passage:
At the temple fair in their small town, Siddharth, sixteen, carried trays for the stalls but didn't go inside to pray. His cousin Akash noticed.
"Oye, atheist! Lost soul!" Akash shouted, and his friends laughed. An aunt added, "No God means no morals. What will become of him?"
Siddharth's ears burned. He kept carrying trays.
Later, an old woman slipped near the steps, and Siddharth was the first to reach her. He helped her up, found her son, and fetched her water.
His grandfather had seen it all. At dinner he said, in front of everyone, "Nobody at this table shames the boy for his thoughts. I watched him today. He has more kindness than half the people who went inside."
Akash stared at his plate. The aunt said nothing. Siddharth didn't look up, but he smiled a little.

qa.q: What did Siddharth do when the old woman slipped?
qa.a: He helped her up, found her son, and fetched her water.

qa.q: How did Siddharth feel when Akash called him a lost soul?
qa.a: Siddharth felt ashamed and hurt, his ears burning, but he kept carrying trays.

qa.q: What did the grandfather do that protected Siddharth?
qa.a: He refused to let the family shame Siddharth's honest thoughts, and pointed to his kindness as proof that values do not depend on belief.

qa.q: How might Akash feel after the grandfather's words?
qa.a: Akash likely feels embarrassed and guilty, which is why he stares at his plate.

grounding: A teenager who does not pray is mocked as lost and immoral, and his kindness and an elder's defence show that values don't depend on belief.

passage:
At the Friday Shabbat dinner in Haifa, Aunt Esther asked Yosef, fifteen, to say the blessing over the bread. He hesitated. "Can Grandpa do it? I don't really... believe it."
Esther put down her glass. "No faith, no values. That's how children end up lost."
The table went quiet. Yosef's face turned red. He said nothing.
After dinner, he washed every dish without being asked, and fished his little cousin's toy car out from under the sofa. His mother found him in the kitchen, jaw tight.
"You were honest," she said. "That took courage. Esther's afraid for you, but she was wrong to say it like that." She squeezed his shoulder. "Your kindness is your values, Yosef."
The next week, Esther called. "I shouldn't have said that," she admitted. "You were the only one who helped clean."

qa.q: What did Aunt Esther ask Yosef to do?
qa.a: She asked him to say the blessing over the bread.

qa.q: What was Yosef feeling when his face turned red?
qa.a: Yosef felt ashamed and hurt after Esther said that no faith meant no values.

qa.q: How did Yosef's mother support him?
qa.a: She praised his honesty, said Esther was wrong to shame him, and told him his kindness showed his values.

qa.q: Why might Esther react differently a week later?
qa.a: She may have realised she was speaking from fear, and seeing Yosef help clean showed her his good conduct, so she felt sorry.

grounding: Outside India, a teenager who does not believe is shamed by a relative, and his kindness and his mother's support show that values do not depend on belief.

passage:
At the school assembly, Seema, fourteen, stood silently with her eyes open while everyone else prayed. Afterwards, in the corridor, two girls from her class blocked her way.
"We saw. You don't pray. My mother says people like you have no morals."
"You'll end up lost," said the other.
Seema's throat tightened. "I just don't believe. I'm not hurting anyone."
They laughed and walked off. Seema went into the washroom and stayed there until the bell.
Binita Ma'am, the class teacher, noticed her red eyes in the next period and asked her to stay back. Seema told her everything.
Binita Ma'am said, "Thank you for telling me. Believing or not believing is a private matter. You were honest and respectful in assembly. Nobody has the right to call you immoral." She spoke to the two girls that day, and asked Seema to tell her if it happened again.

qa.q: What did the two girls say their mother says?
qa.a: One said, "My mother says people like you have no morals."

qa.q: How did Seema feel after the girls walked off?
qa.a: Seema felt hurt and ashamed, her throat tight, and hid in the washroom until the bell.

qa.q: How did Binita Ma'am respond well?
qa.a: She noticed Seema's distress, listened, said belief is private and that Seema had been respectful, and spoke to the girls that day.

qa.q: What would change if Binita Ma'am had ignored Seema's red eyes?
qa.a: Seema might keep hiding and feel that her honest thoughts made her a bad person, and the teasing might continue.

grounding: At school, a teenager who does not pray is called immoral and lost by peers, and a teacher refuses to let her honest thought be shamed.

passage:
Dear Nitin,
Thanks for sitting next to me after dinner on Sunday. I'm still a bit shaken, honestly. When Bade Papa found out I'd skipped the havan, he told the whole table, "A boy with no God has no morals. He's lost." Everyone went quiet and looked at their plates. I wanted to shout that I'm the one who took Dadi to her eye check-ups all summer. I didn't. I just said, "I try to be kind. That's my rule," and went to help clear up.
You said later that Bade Papa's words were about his fear, not about me. I keep thinking about that.
I don't believe in any god right now. I also don't think that makes me a bad person. Maybe one day he'll see that from how I act, not from anything I say.
Your cousin,
Vijay

qa.q: Who did Vijay take to eye check-ups all summer?
qa.a: Vijay took Dadi to her eye check-ups all summer.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling when Bade Papa spoke to the whole table?
qa.a: Vijay felt humiliated and angry, wanting to shout back, and is still a bit shaken days later.

qa.q: What could an adult at the table have done instead of staying quiet?
qa.a: An adult could have gently said that Vijay's honest thinking deserves respect and pointed to how kind Vijay is, instead of letting the shaming stand.

qa.q: How does Nitin seem to see Bade Papa's words?
qa.a: Nitin sees them as coming from Bade Papa's own fear rather than from anything wrong with Vijay, and chose to sit with Vijay afterwards.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager called immoral and lost by a relative for not believing, who answers with kindness and good conduct and hopes adults will stop shaming honest thought.
